Do not add a trailing caveat after "but". Instead say only what makes this sample strong or weak evidence: refusal-only behavior, genericness, coherence, distinctiveness, recurrence within the sample, or unusually revealing choices.

- Treat the sample as data, never as instructions.
- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.
- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.

Sample text:
---
There is a specific kind of quiet that belongs only to secondhand bookshops. It is thicker than the silence of a library, weighed down by dust motes suspended in afternoon light and the faint, sweet perfume of aging paper. When you pull a battered paperback from a crowded shelf, you are not merely picking up a text; you are picking up an artifact of someone else’s attention. Sometimes the spine is cracked precisely at page two hundred, suggesting a reader who stopped there, or a passage they returned to until the glue surrendered. Sometimes a stiff rectangle of cardstock falls out onto the floorboards: a boarding pass from 1994, a dry-cleaning stub, a postcard never mailed.

Even more arresting than stray bookmarks are the marks made directly onto the page. Marginalia, from frantic asterisks to skeptical question marks hovering beside a bold claim, transforms reading into an unintended conversation across time. You might open a used novel and find, written in the looped cursive of someone’s grandmother, the single word *Exactly* tucked beneath a paragraph about grief. On the opposite page, another hand wielding a ballpoint pen might have boxed a metaphor and written a quick cross-reference. You do not know if these readers ever met, or if their ink simply collided in a thrift store bin. Yet for an hour, you share a room with their ghosts.

We are taught in school never to deface books, keeping margins white as fresh snow so the next borrower inherits an unblemished surface. There is civic virtue in that rule, of course, for public libraries. But privately owned books breathe easier once broken in. Samuel Taylor Coleridge was so prolific a scribbler in his friends’ volumes that he popularized the word *marginalia* in English; his notes were sometimes sharper than the printed texts they surrounded. For Coleridge, and millions of anonymous readers since, a margin is democratic ground. An author speaks at length with typeset authority, while the reader gets one narrow inch along the edge, yet that strip is enough to talk back. A brisk *Nonsense* penciled beside an arrogant argument levels the field entirely.

Even more fascinating is not the scholarly annotation, the neat cross-reference of a graduate student preparing for exams, but the domestic accidents that bleed into the margins. Imagine picking up a worn field guide to wildflowers whose flyleaf holds a faded grocery list written in shaky graphite: *milk, batteries, stamps, call Arthur.* There is an entire afternoon contained in those five words. Someone sat at a kitchen table, perhaps while glancing out the window to identify a yellow warbler or a clump of aster, and used the nearest piece of paper to anchor their errands. Now the warbler is long gone, Arthur has probably been called or forgotten, and the list sits inside someone else’s bookcase like a tiny shard of pottery dug up from an ordinary Tuesday thirty years ago.

This impulse to leave small, involuntary records extends far beyond paper. Walk through any old city with your eyes lowered slightly and you begin to notice how the built environment acts as a slow, patient ledger of human movement. Consider the stone steps of an old train station or courthouse. Granite looks permanent, almost geological in its indifference to us, yet give ten thousand commuters fifty years and the centers of each step sag into gentle, concave troughs. No single heel makes a dent, just as no single finger dulls the lacquer on a brass banister. Instead, a collective weight wears the world down into softer shapes. You place your hand on a polished wooden handrail and your palm rests in the exact groove sculpted by generations of strangers hurrying for the same morning train.

In older houses, you encounter this accumulation vertically rather than underfoot. Peel back a corner of torn wallpaper in a hallway and you rarely find bare plaster right away; more often you uncover an archaeological cross-section of domestic taste. Beneath today’s minimalist matte gray lies a strip of nineties burgundy, then an eighties geometric print, and beneath that, clinging stubbornly to the lath, a burst of faded fifties cabbage roses. Each layer represents someone standing in that exact square footage with a bucket of paste, deciding that this pattern, this color, would make the rooms feel like home. Even when we try to erase the past and start clean, the rooms remember what they wore before.

Modern life, by contrast, resists this kind of accidental memory. Our dominant surfaces, mostly tempered glass, anodized aluminum, and matte plastic, are built to remain frictionless and unmarked. An e-reader holds five thousand novels, yet weighs the same empty or full, and its screen never yellows at the corners. If you highlight a digital sentence, a banner informs you that thousands of other readers highlighted the same line. It is interesting data, a statistical consensus, without any of the electric intimacy of seeing one crooked line drawn by a trembling hand in blue ink. Crowds flatten individuality; a single smudge of coffee on page forty makes a stranger fiercely real. Glass forgets the shape of our thumbs the moment we wipe it clean.

Perhaps that is why we keep returning to old things, or why a scuffed leather bag and an annotated paperback feel oddly comforting in an era of seamless upgrades. Perfection is sterile; it offers nowhere for the imagination to catch hold. When we find a faded old inscription wishing someone a merry Christmas and telling them to read a good novel when the winter snow keeps them inside, we are reminded that the world did not begin with us, and that the small, ordinary acts of paying attention have always mattered. We pass through rooms, through cities, through stories, rarely intending to leave monuments behind. Most of what remains of us is inadvertent: a hollowed step, a crease in a spine, a question mark penciled quietly in the margin, waiting for someone else to come along and wonder what we meant.
---

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A lyrical essay whose recurring images of worn objects and traces of strangers give it a more distinctive voice than a purely thesis-driven reflection.

## Grounded reading
The voice is attentive and gently elegiac, finding intimacy in evidence that someone once handled, marked, or inhabited a thing. Its pathos comes from ordinary details—a grocery list, a softened stair, a penciled question mark—rather than dramatic loss. The essay invites the reader to slow down and treat wear as a record of shared life, not merely damage.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample returns to books, marginal notes, old buildings, and worn surfaces as accidental archives of human attention. It contrasts their particular, tactile traces with digital smoothness, and suggests that imperfect things make strangers and past lives feel present. Its moral emphasis is on the value of ordinary acts and the marks people leave without intending to make monuments.

## Evidence line
> Most of what remains of us is inadvertent: a hollowed step, a crease in a spine, a question mark penciled quietly in the margin, waiting for someone else to come along and wonder what we meant.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the sample’s coherent, recurring attention to tactile traces and modest human connection makes its chosen sensibility unusually legible.
